questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with colon adenocarcinoma. Researchers analyzing his tumor find that the malignant cells express an enzyme that is essentially absent from his normal somatic cells, maintains the ends of chromosomes, and prevents the replicative senescence that normally limits cell division. This enzyme is expressed in the vast majority of human cancers. Which of the following best classifies this tumor antigen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oncogenic viral protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neoantigen produced by a point mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aberrantly-expressed self-protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Product of a mutated proto-oncogene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alloantigen recognized by preformed antibodies

explanation.summary: Telomerase is a normal self-protein abnormally expressed by most cancers, halting the telomere shortening seen in senescence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists telomerase as the example of an aberrantly-expressed self-protein: it is expressed in the vast majority of cancers and halts the normal telomere shortening that occurs in senescence. Because it is a normal protein expressed abnormally (rather than a mutated or viral product), it is categorized as an aberrantly-expressed self-protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oncogenic viral proteins come from cancer-causing viruses such as HPV; telomerase is an endogenous human enzyme, not a viral product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A neoantigen arises from a mutation that changes a self-protein; telomerase here is not mutated but simply expressed abnormally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oncogene products come from mutated proto-oncogenes; telomerase re-expression is not described as an oncogene product in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alloantigens and preformed antibodies belong to transplant rejection, not tumor antigen classification.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A melanoma is found to have downregulated its class I MHC molecules so that it can no longer present tumor-associated peptides to cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Despite this, the tumor is still attacked by a population of lymphocytes. Which cell is now the dominant effector against this tumor, and how does it recognize the malignant cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognizing peptide presented on MHC class II

choices.label: B
choices.text: Natural killer cells recognizing stress-associated signals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma cells producing neutralizing antibodies against the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Th1 cells presenting tumor antigen on their own MHC class I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory T cells inducing tolerance to the tumor

explanation.summary: When tumor-associated antigens cannot be presented on MHC class I, NK cells become the dominant effector because they act independently of MHC I.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that if tumor-associated antigens cannot be presented by MHC I, NK cells make up the dominant immune response. NK cells recognize abnormal cells independent of MHC I by detecting stress-associated molecular signals or surface-bound IgG, so loss of MHC I does not blind them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLs recognize peptide on MHC class I, not class II, and their response fails precisely because MHC I is downregulated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The dominant anti-tumor response described is cell-mediated (CTLs and NK cells), not antibody-mediated by plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Th1 cells do not present tumor antigen on MHC I to kill tumor cells; they help coordinate responses via cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses rather than serve as the dominant anti-tumor effector.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with cervical carcinoma associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Her oncologist explains that specific viral proteins are helping the tumor grow. By which mechanism do these oncogenic HPV proteins promote the survival of cancer cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They interact with p53 and help prevent apoptosis of cancer cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They activate telomerase to lengthen telomeres directly

choices.label: C
choices.text: They downregulate class I MHC to hide from cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They secrete TGF-beta to suppress Th1 cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They trigger antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity against the tumor

explanation.summary: HPV is an oncogenic virus whose proteins interact with p53 and help block apoptosis of cancer cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explicitly states that cancer can be caused by viruses like HPV, and that HPV proteins interact with p53 (described as an oncogene) and help prevent apoptosis of cancer cells. Blocking apoptosis allows the malignant cells to survive and proliferate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Telomerase re-expression is a separate aberrant self-protein mechanism, not the described action of HPV proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC class I downregulation is a general tumor evasion (low immunogenicity) strategy, not the specific HPV mechanism taught here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta suppression of Th1 cells is a tumor immune-suppression mechanism, not an action of HPV proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ADCC is an immune effector mechanism that damages tumors; it is not how HPV proteins promote cancer survival.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A pathologist examining a solid tumor notes that immune cells are largely excluded from the tumor mass by a dense barrier of secreted extracellular matrix. The few lymphocytes that do infiltrate are found to be functionally inactivated by a ligand the tumor has upregulated on its surface. Which tumor evasion strategy is illustrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low immunogenicity through MHC class I downregulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigenic modulation through ADCC-based selection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune privilege through an extracellular matrix barrier and PD-L1 upregulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance from presenting antigen without co-stimulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune suppression through TGF-beta and IL-10 secretion

explanation.summary: Creating an immune-privileged site uses secreted extracellular matrix to block access and PD-L1 to inactivate infiltrating immune cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes immune privilege as tumors secreting extracellular matrix components to physically block immune cell access to the tumor and upregulating PD-L1 to inactivate any immune cells that do infiltrate. Both features in this vignette match that strategy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low immunogenicity involves downregulating MHC I, adhesion, and co-stimulatory molecules, not building an ECM barrier or using PD-L1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigenic modulation selects for cells lacking a targeted antigen via antibody-mediated ADCC, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral tolerance results from presenting self-peptide without co-stimulation; it does not involve a physical ECM barrier or PD-L1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune suppression via TGF-beta and IL-10 shifts cytokine and cell populations rather than physically excluding and inactivating infiltrating cells.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: Analysis of a tumor microenvironment reveals abundant regulatory T cells and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages, suppression of Th1 cells and M1 macrophages, and decreased expression of activating receptors on nearby NK cells. Which pair of cytokines is most critical to this immune-suppressive state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: TGF-beta and IL-10

choices.label: B
choices.text: IFN-gamma and IL-12

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perforin and granzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-2 and TNF-alpha

choices.label: E
choices.text: C3a and C5a

explanation.summary: TGF-beta and IL-10 are the cytokines the brick names as critical to tumor-driven immune suppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that TGF-beta and IL-10 are cytokines critical for immune suppression, producing suppression of M1 macrophages with induction of M2s, suppression of Th1 cells with induction of regulatory T cells, and decreased activating receptors on NK cells, exactly the picture described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-gamma and IL-12 are pro-inflammatory cytokines that activate NK cells and Th1 responses, the opposite of the suppressive state shown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perforin and granzyme are cytotoxic effector molecules used by CTLs and NK cells to kill targets, not suppressive cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-2 and TNF-alpha promote immune activation rather than the suppression described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C3a and C5a are complement anaphylatoxins that recruit and activate inflammatory cells, not tumor immune-suppression cytokines.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with severe aortic valve disease undergoes valve replacement using tissue derived from a pig. Which term best describes this type of graft?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autograft

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isograft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allograft

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xenograft

choices.label: E
choices.text: Syngraft

explanation.summary: A graft transferred between different species, such as a pig valve into a human, is a xenograft.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines xenografts as grafts between species, giving the example of pig heart valves, where 'xeno' means foreign. A pig-derived valve implanted in a human is therefore a xenograft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autograft is within the same person (self to self), such as skin moved from thigh to chest.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An isograft is between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An allograft is between genetically different people of the same species, not between species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Syngraft is not one of the four graft categories taught in the brick; the correct term for a between-species graft is xenograft.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A transplant team evaluating a potential kidney donor and recipient places heavy emphasis on matching the genes that encode human leukocyte antigens (HLA). Which statement best explains why this matching is prioritized?

choices.label: A
choices.text: MHC genes are highly polymorphic

choices.label: B
choices.text: MHC molecules are identical across all humans, so matching is only a formality

choices.label: C
choices.text: Matching MHC prevents graft-versus-host disease in all solid organ transplants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only ABO blood group, not MHC, influences solid organ rejection

choices.label: E
choices.text: MHC class I is encoded by the beta-1 locus and rarely varies between people

explanation.summary: MHC genes are among the most polymorphic in the genome, so the closer the donor-recipient match, the lower the alloimmune response and the better the transplant odds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that MHC genes are highly polymorphic and are the genes seen to be most critical to match between donor and recipient to prevent an immune response. It states that the closer the blood and MHC match, the better the odds of a successful transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC molecules are not identical across humans; they are highly polymorphic, which is precisely why matching matters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Matching reduces rejection, but graft-versus-host disease is a distinct problem tied to donor immune cells, not something MHC matching prevents in all solid organ transplants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both ABO blood group and MHC influence transplant outcome; MHC matching is specifically stressed as critical.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I is matched at the alpha loci and is highly polymorphic; it is the beta-1 loci that pertain to class II, and neither rarely varies.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman receives a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Within minutes of restoring blood flow, the graft becomes mottled and dusky. Biopsy shows platelet-fibrin thrombi, neutrophil accumulation, complement (C4d) deposition on the endothelium, and severe ischemic injury. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preformed recipient antibodies binding donor alloantigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recipient cytotoxic T cell-mediated apoptosis of graft cells developing over weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helper T cell-driven smooth muscle proliferation over several years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Donor T cells recognizing and attacking recipient tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity building up over several days

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours from preformed recipient antibodies against donor alloantigens that activate complement and inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes hyperacute rejection (a type 2 hypersensitivity) as occurring within minutes to 24 hours, mediated by preformed recipient antibodies specific to donor alloantigens. These trigger complement activation, with C4d and C3d deposition, membrane attack complexes, and Fc-mediated inflammation, producing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis, exactly as shown.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CTL-mediated apoptosis of graft cells over weeks describes acute rejection, not a reaction occurring within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helper T cell-driven smooth muscle proliferation is chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues describes graft-versus-host disease, not rejection of the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A type IV delayed hypersensitivity building over days does not match a reaction that begins within minutes of reperfusion.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man who received a kidney transplant three weeks ago develops a rising serum creatinine. A graft biopsy shows a dense interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes resembling vasculitis. Which mechanism most likely underlies this rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recipient cytotoxic T cells recognizing alloantigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preformed antibodies and complement causing injury within minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arteriosclerosis from chronic helper T cell cytokines over years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Donor lymphocytes attacking the recipient's skin and gut

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity to graft antigens

explanation.summary: Acute rejection occurs about one week to several months post-transplant and features recipient CTLs recognizing alloantigens on donor MHC I, with a lymphocyte-rich vasculitis-like picture.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states acute rejection occurs one week to several months after transplant and that recipient CTLs recognize alloantigens presented on donor MHC I to induce apoptosis of graft cells. Histologically the graft resembles vasculitis with a dense interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes, matching this three-week presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Preformed antibody and complement injury within minutes is hyperacute rejection, not a reaction at three weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Arteriosclerosis from chronic helper T cell cytokines is chronic rejection, which unfolds over months to years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Donor lymphocytes attacking recipient skin and gut describes graft-versus-host disease, not rejection of the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is not the mechanism of acute cellular rejection described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman who received a lung transplant three years ago has slowly progressive graft dysfunction. Biopsy reveals arteriosclerosis of graft vessels and thickened small airways with fibrosis. Which mechanism best accounts for this pattern of chronic rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recipient helper T cell cytokines stimulating vascular smooth muscle proliferation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preformed antibodies causing immediate thrombosis of the graft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor NK cells lysing the recipient's enterocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complement-mediated membrane attack complexes forming within 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity to inhaled allergens

explanation.summary: Chronic rejection develops over months to years as recipient helper T cell cytokines drive vascular smooth muscle proliferation, producing arteriosclerosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that chronic rejection occurs months to years after transplant, likely from recipient helper T cells recognizing alloantigens on MHC II, whose cytokines (IFN-gamma and others) stimulate proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells. The resulting arteriosclerosis compromises graft blood flow, and lung transplants specifically show thickened small airways.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Preformed antibodies causing immediate thrombosis is hyperacute rejection occurring within minutes to 24 hours, not years later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor NK cells lysing recipient enterocytes describes graft-versus-host disease, not chronic rejection of the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rapid complement-mediated MAC formation within 24 hours is a hyperacute mechanism, not the slow arteriosclerotic process of chronic rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I hypersensitivity to inhaled allergens is unrelated to the alloimmune helper T cell mechanism of chronic rejection.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia receives an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant from an unrelated donor after conditioning chemotherapy. Several weeks later she develops a maculopapular rash, jaundice, and intractable diarrhea. Blood tests are otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graft-versus-host disease mediated by donor T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperacute rejection from preformed recipient antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute rejection of the graft by recipient cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic rejection with graft arteriosclerosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrence of leukemia

explanation.summary: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor immune cells recognize recipient tissues as foreign, classically affecting skin, liver, and GI tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes GVHD as occurring with allogeneic stem cell transplants when donor immune cells mount a response against the recipient, with donor T cells as the primary effectors and CTLs and NK cells causing tissue damage. It most commonly affects skin, liver, and GI tract, presenting with maculopapular rash, jaundice, and diarrhea, precisely this patient's picture.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperacute rejection is the recipient's preformed antibodies attacking a solid organ graft within minutes, not a weeks-later multi-organ syndrome after stem cell transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute rejection is the recipient attacking the graft; here the donor cells are attacking the recipient's own tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic rejection causes graft arteriosclerosis over years and does not explain rash, jaundice, and diarrhea a few weeks post-transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood tests are otherwise normal with no indication of relapse; the rash, jaundice, and diarrhea point to GVHD rather than recurrent leukemia.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: In a classic experiment, a mouse rejects a skin allograft from an unrelated donor about 14 days after grafting. Weeks later, the same mouse receives a second skin graft from the same donor and rejects it in only about 6 days. Which principle best explains the accelerated second rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immunologic memory to the donor's alloantigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preformed antibodies that were present before any transplant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of MHC matching on the second graft

choices.label: D
choices.text: Graft-versus-host disease caused by donor memory cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development of tolerance to the donor after the first graft

explanation.summary: Because the adaptive immune response generates memory, a repeat graft sharing alloantigens is rejected faster (second-set rejection).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that adaptive immune responses generate memory, so allografts generate memory to alloantigens, and additional allografts from the same donor (or donors with similar alloantigens) are rejected faster. The 6-day second-set rejection reflects memory cells formed during the first (14-day) rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Preformed antibodies present before any transplant would cause hyperacute rejection of the first graft as well; here the first graft took 14 days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both grafts came from the same donor with the same MHC, so a change in matching is not the cause of the faster rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Graft-versus-host disease involves donor cells attacking the host; this scenario is host rejection of donor skin, accelerated by host memory.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance would make the second graft survive longer, not be rejected faster.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with end-stage renal disease receives a kidney donated by his identical twin brother. Which of the following best describes this graft and its expected immunologic consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autograft; the graft introduces no foreign antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isograft; the graft introduces no foreign antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allograft; a hypersensitivity reaction to alloantigens is expected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xenograft; preformed antibodies will bind the graft within hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Allograft; the graft introduces no foreign antigens

explanation.summary: A graft between genetically identical people (twins) is an isograft, and because no foreign antigens are introduced, a hypersensitivity reaction is not expected.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines isografts as grafts between genetically identical people such as twins ('iso' = identical). It also states that unless the graft is an autograft or isograft, any graft exposes the immune system to foreign antigens and a hypersensitivity reaction is possible; an isograft from an identical twin therefore introduces no foreign antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autograft is tissue moved within the same person ('auto' = self), such as skin from the leg to the chest, not tissue from a twin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An allograft is between genetically different people; identical twins are genetically identical, so no alloantigens are introduced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is between species (e.g., pig heart valves); a human twin donor is not a xenograft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although an allograft is the most common graft in the United States, it is defined by genetic difference and does expose the recipient to foreign antigens.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with blood group A is mistakenly transfused with group B red blood cells and develops immediate agglutination of the transfused cells. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recipient Th1 cells releasing cytokines that recruit neutrophils and macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recipient cytotoxic T cells recognizing alloantigens on donor MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isoagglutinins in her plasma directed against ABO antigens she does not express

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory cells formed during an earlier graft from a donor with similar alloantigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viable donor lymphocytes engrafting and mounting a response against her tissues

explanation.summary: People often have antibodies (isoagglutinins) against ABO antigens they lack, and these cause transfused cells with different ABO genes to agglutinate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that ABO blood group genes are critical for preventing an immune response in transplantation. People often have antibodies against antigens they do not have; these antibodies, called isoagglutinins, cause blood transfusions from people with different ABO genes to agglutinate. A group A recipient's isoagglutinins against the B antigen explain the immediate agglutination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Th1 cytokine-driven recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages is an acute rejection mechanism and does not agglutinate red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CTL recognition of alloantigens on donor MHC class I is the direct cytotoxicity mechanism of acute rejection, which takes a week or more, not an immediate agglutination reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Memory to alloantigens accelerates rejection of a repeat graft; this patient's reaction is due to preexisting isoagglutinins, not a prior graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Engraftment of viable donor lymphocytes causes transfusion-associated GVHD, a delayed multisystem disorder, not immediate agglutination of the transfused cells.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A transplant immunologist explains to a medical student that only certain regions of the MHC molecules require the closest possible match between donor and recipient, because these regions carry the greatest number of alleles in the population. Which of the following pairs identifies those regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-2 and alpha-3 loci of class I MHC and beta-2 locus of class II MHC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-1 and alpha-2 loci of class I MHC and beta-1 locus of class II MHC

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-1 and alpha-3 loci of class I MHC and alpha-1 locus of class II MHC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alpha-2 and alpha-3 loci of class I MHC and alpha-2 locus of class II MHC

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alpha-1 and alpha-2 loci of class I MHC and beta-2 locus of class II MHC

explanation.summary: The alpha-1 and alpha-2 loci of class I MHC and the beta-1 locus of class II MHC are the most polymorphic regions and the most critical to match in transplantation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that two groups of MHC genes seem most critical to match between donor and recipient to prevent an immune response: the alpha-1 and alpha-2 loci for class I MHC and the beta-1 loci for class II MHC. These are also the most polymorphic regions, as shown by the variability plots in the brick's figure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The class I alpha-3 region and class II beta-2 region show comparatively little variability and are not the critical matching regions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Class I alpha-3 is one of the least variable regions, and the class II region that matters is beta-1, not alpha-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither class I alpha-3 nor class II alpha-2 is identified as highly polymorphic; class I needs alpha-1 and alpha-2, and class II needs beta-1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The class I alpha-1 and alpha-2 loci are correct, but class II beta-2 is a low-variability region; the critical class II locus is beta-1.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: During hyperacute rejection of a transplanted kidney, complement activation on the graft endothelium generates fragments that attract and activate neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils. Which of the following are those fragments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C3a and C5a

choices.label: B
choices.text: C4d and C3d

choices.label: C
choices.text: C5b through C9

choices.label: D
choices.text: C1 complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG and IgM

explanation.summary: C3a and C5a are generated during complement activation in hyperacute rejection and attract and activate neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the complement effector mechanisms of hyperacute rejection: C4d and C3d are deposited on transplanted cells for opsonization, C3a and C5a are generated and attract and activate neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils, and membrane attack complexes punch holes in membranes. The chemoattractant and activating fragments are therefore C3a and C5a.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C4d and C3d are deposited on transplanted cells to mark them for destruction by phagocytes (opsonization), not to attract inflammatory cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C5b-C9 forms the membrane attack complex, which damages cells by punching holes in their membranes rather than recruiting leukocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The C1 complex binds recipient IgG or IgM to initiate the classical pathway; it is the trigger, not the chemoattractant product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgG and IgM are the preformed recipient antibodies that start the cascade; they are not complement fragments.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A biopsy of a hyperacutely rejected renal allograft shows neutrophils, monocytes, and NK cells bound to antibody-coated endothelium and releasing reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, perforin, and granzymes. Which of the following best describes how these inflammatory cells were engaged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemotaxis toward IFN-gamma released by Th1 cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: T cell receptor recognition of alloantigen on donor MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phagocytic uptake of cells opsonized by C4d and C3d

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding of IgG through Fc receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recognition of stress-associated signals independent of antibody

explanation.summary: In Fc-mediated inflammation, neutrophils, monocytes, and NK cells bind IgG through Fc receptors and injure the graft with ROS, RNS, perforin, and granzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names two major effector mechanisms of hyperacute rejection: complement activation and Fc-mediated inflammation. In the latter, neutrophils, monocytes, and NK cells bind IgG via Fc receptors and injure the transplant by releasing reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, perforin, and granzymes, exactly as seen in this biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Th1 cytokine recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages is an acute rejection mechanism that develops over a week or more, not within the minutes-to-hours window of hyperacute rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TCR recognition of alloantigen on donor MHC class I is the direct cytotoxicity of acute rejection by CTLs, and neutrophils, monocytes, and NK cells do not use a TCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4d and C3d opsonization marks cells for phagocytosis; the cells here are engaged by antibody itself and are releasing cytotoxic mediators rather than phagocytosing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK cells can recognize stress signals independent of antibody, but in this antibody-coated graft the cells are bound to IgG, which is the Fc receptor mechanism.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: During a kidney transplant operation, shortly after the vascular anastomosis is completed, the surgeon notes that the graft turns dusky and shows early signs of necrosis before the incision is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an immunosuppressive drug that inhibits mTOR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the dose of calcineurin inhibitor and observe

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gamma-irradiate the graft to inactivate donor lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wait 5 to 8 days for alloantigen-specific effector cells to form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove the graft as soon as possible

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection is so severe and rapid that the graft may necrose during surgery, and the graft must be removed as soon as possible.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that hyperacute rejection ultimately causes ischemia and necrosis, that the reaction is so severe and rapid that the graft may show signs of necrosis during the transplantation surgery, and that in cases of hyperacute rejection the graft must be removed as soon as possible.

whyWrongByChoice.A: mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus are part of maintenance immunosuppression and do not reverse hyperacute rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppressive drugs prevent T cell-driven rejection and GVHD; they cannot undo preformed-antibody and complement-mediated necrosis already under way.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gamma-irradiation is used on blood products to prevent transfusion-associated GVHD by disabling donor lymphocytes; it has no role in a necrosing solid organ graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 5 to 8 day lag applies to the generation of effector T cells and antibodies in acute rejection; hyperacute rejection is driven by preformed antibodies and is already destroying the graft.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: Two months after kidney transplantation, a 50-year-old man develops rejection. The biopsy shows CD8+ T cell-mediated damage to parenchymal cells together with alloantibody deposition on the endothelium and endothelialitis. Which hypersensitivity reaction types are primarily responsible for this rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type 1 and type 3

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type 2 only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2 and type 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 3 and type 4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 4 only

explanation.summary: Acute rejection is primarily mediated by type 2 (antibody against cell-associated antigen) and type 4 (T cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acute rejection occurs 1 week to several months after transplant and is primarily mediated by type 2 and type 4 HSRs. Its effector mechanisms are direct CTL cytotoxicity and Th1 cytokines (type 4) plus alloantibodies that bind vascular endothelium (type 2), matching the combined cell damage and endothelialitis on this biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 reactions are IgE responses to allergens and type 3 reactions target soluble antigens; neither is the primary mechanism of graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperacute rejection is primarily a type 2 HSR alone; acute rejection adds T cell-mediated (type 4) damage, which is evident here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 reactions involve soluble antigen immune complexes, whereas graft alloantigens are cell- or tissue-associated (type 2).
whyWrongByChoice.E: The alloantibody deposition and endothelialitis represent a type 2 antibody-mediated component in addition to the type 4 T cell damage.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: Three weeks after heart transplantation, a biopsy of the graft shows an infiltrate of neutrophils and macrophages recruited and activated by cytokines from recipient Th1 cells. Which of the following cells presented the alloantigens that activated these Th1 cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recipient APCs that migrated into the graft, on MHC class II

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor parenchymal cells within the graft, on MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor endothelial cells lining graft vessels, on MHC class II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recipient B cells in the spleen, on MHC class I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Donor macrophages carried inside the graft, on MHC class II

explanation.summary: In the Th1 cytokine arm of acute rejection, recipient Th1 cells recognize alloantigens presented on MHC class II by recipient APCs that have migrated into donor tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the Th1 cytokine mechanism of acute rejection: recipient Th1 cells recognize alloantigens presented on MHC II on recipient antigen-presenting cells that have migrated into donor tissues. Activated Th1 cells then release cytokines that recruit neutrophils and macrophages and promote their activation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor parenchymal cells presenting alloantigen on donor MHC class I are the targets of recipient CTLs in direct cytotoxicity, not the activators of Th1 cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor endothelial cells are the surfaces bound by alloantibodies in the antibody-mediated arm; Th1 activation is described via recipient APCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I does not present to helper T cells, and the brick locates the presenting recipient APCs within the donor tissue rather than the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick specifies that the presenting cells are recipient APCs that migrated into the graft, not donor-derived macrophages.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman receives a kidney transplant. Testing before surgery showed no recipient antibodies against the donor. Four weeks later she develops graft dysfunction, and biopsy shows antibody and complement deposition on the vascular endothelium with thrombosis. Which of the following best explains why this antibody-mediated injury appeared weeks rather than minutes after transplantation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor MHC class I had to be downregulated before antibody binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preformed isoagglutinins were consumed and had to be slowly regenerated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complement was depleted by surgery and slowly restored

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alloantibodies against the donor formed only after the transplant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Memory cells from an earlier graft required weeks of reactivation

explanation.summary: Antibody-mediated acute rejection uses the same mechanism as hyperacute rejection but occurs later because the alloantibodies form after transplantation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes antibody-mediated responses in acute rejection: alloantibodies that form after transplantation bind alloantigens on vascular endothelial cells. The mechanism of damage is equivalent to hyperacute rejection but occurs later due to the time it takes to form an antibody response. With no antibodies detected before surgery, the injury at four weeks reflects newly formed alloantibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alloantibodies bind alloantigens on the endothelial surface; downregulation of MHC class I is a tumor evasion strategy, not a prerequisite for antibody binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isoagglutinins are preexisting ABO antibodies that would cause immediate agglutination and hyperacute injury, not a delayed response; pre-transplant testing showed no antibodies against the donor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe complement depletion by surgery; the delay reflects antibody formation, not complement availability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no earlier graft in this history, and memory would produce faster, not delayed, rejection.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man receives a liver transplant from a donor with many mismatched alloantigens. Serial biopsies during the first 4 days show no lymphocytic infiltrate and no alloantibody deposition. Which of the following best explains the absence of acute rejection during this period?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The liver secretes extracellular matrix that blocks lymphocyte entry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alloantigens are not expressed on graft cells until the second week after surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Effector T cells and antibodies take at least 5 to 8 days to be generated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preformed antibodies neutralize alloantigens during the first week

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recipient APCs cannot enter the graft until the vessels heal

explanation.summary: Acute rejection is mediated by effector T cells and antibodies formed after transplantation, which take at least 5 to 8 days to generate because of T and B cell activation requirements.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acute rejection is mediated by effector T cells and antibodies formed following transplantation, and that these immune components take at least 5 to 8 days to be generated due to the requirements of T and B cell activation. Acute rejection therefore begins about 1 week to several months after transplant, so day 4 biopsies are expected to be clear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secreting extracellular matrix to block immune access is a tumor immune-privilege strategy, not a property of a transplanted liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alloantigens such as donor MHC are present on graft cells from the start; the delay lies in the recipient's adaptive response, not antigen expression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preformed antibodies would cause hyperacute rejection within minutes to 24 hours rather than protecting the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes recipient APCs migrating into donor tissue as part of acute rejection but does not tie this to vessel healing; the limiting step is lymphocyte activation.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant is discharged on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone to prevent rejection. Collectively, the medicines commonly given after organ transplantation act by inhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ABO antigen expression on graft endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: C1 complex binding and membrane attack complex formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fc receptor expression on neutrophils and NK cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telomerase activity and telomere shortening

choices.label: E
choices.text: NF-kB, mTOR, calcineurin, and lymphocyte proliferation

explanation.summary: Post-transplant immunosuppressants collectively inhibit NF-kB, mTOR, calcineurin, lymphocyte proliferation, and cytokine production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation lists azathioprine, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, sirolimus, and tacrolimus as common medicines after organ transplantation and states that collectively they inhibit NF-kB, mTOR, calcineurin, lymphocyte proliferation, and cytokine production, preventing transplant-related HSRs (rejection or GVHD).

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABO antigens are matched before transplantation; they are not a target of immunosuppressive drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C1 binding and MAC formation are complement events in hyperacute rejection; the listed drugs target lymphocyte signaling and proliferation, not complement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fc receptor binding by neutrophils and NK cells drives Fc-mediated inflammation, but the brick does not describe these drugs as acting on Fc receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Telomerase is an aberrantly expressed self-protein in tumors and is unrelated to transplant immunosuppression.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who received a liver transplant 5 years ago develops progressive cholestasis. Biopsy shows fibrotic, nonfunctional bile ducts and arteriosclerosis of graft vessels. He asks whether increasing his immunosuppressive drugs will restore graft function. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; once fibrosis has occurred the organ is no longer viable

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes; immunosuppressants reverse vascular smooth muscle proliferation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes; the injury is antibody-mediated and resolves with treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: No; this is hyperacute rejection and the graft must be removed today

choices.label: E
choices.text: No; this is graft-versus-host disease and requires donor lymphocyte removal

explanation.summary: Chronic rejection in a liver transplant produces fibrotic, nonfunctional bile ducts; immunosuppressants prevent chronic rejection, but once fibrosis occurs the organ is no longer viable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the pathology of chronic rejection is arteriosclerosis and that its specific changes differ by organ, with chronic rejection in liver transplant showing fibrotic and nonfunctional bile ducts. It adds that immunosuppressive drugs act to prevent chronic rejection; however, once fibrosis occurs, the organ is no longer viable.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppressants are preventive; the brick does not describe them reversing established smooth muscle proliferation or fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic rejection is driven by helper T cell cytokines, not antibodies, and established fibrosis does not resolve with treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours of transplant, not 5 years later with slowly developing fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GVHD is donor immune cells attacking recipient skin, liver, and GI tract; here the recipient's immune response has damaged the graft's own bile ducts and vessels.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman lost her first kidney transplant to acute rejection. Two years later she receives a second kidney from a different, unrelated donor who shares several HLA alleles with the first donor. The second graft is rejected much faster than the first. Which of the following best explains the accelerated rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preformed isoagglutinins against the second donor's ABO antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Memory cells from the first graft recognize the shared alloantigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor lymphocytes carried in the second graft attack her tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suppression of her regulatory T cells by the post-transplant immunosuppressive drugs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic rejection carried over from the first graft's vessels

explanation.summary: Allografts generate memory to alloantigens, so later grafts from the same donor or from other donors with similar alloantigens are rejected faster.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that an adaptive immune response generates memory, so allografts generate memory to alloantigens. Additional allografts from the same donor, or from multiple donors with similar alloantigens, result in faster rejection. Because the second donor shares HLA alleles with the first, the memory formed during the first rejection accelerates rejection of the second graft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isoagglutinins are ABO antibodies unrelated to prior grafts; the stem's cue is shared HLA alleles, not an ABO mismatch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor lymphocytes attacking recipient tissue is GVHD, which causes rash, jaundice, and diarrhea rather than accelerated rejection of the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe immunosuppressants suppressing regulatory T cells to accelerate rejection; they inhibit lymphocyte proliferation and cytokine production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic rejection is a months-to-years process in a given graft's vessels and cannot be transferred from a removed graft to a new one.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man receives a liver transplant. Three weeks later he develops a maculopapular rash and profuse diarrhea, and donor-derived lymphocytes are detected in his circulation. Which of the following best explains why this complication can follow a solid organ transplant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liver grafts require only ABO matching

choices.label: B
choices.text: The liver expresses abundant MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrotic bile ducts release inflammatory cytokines

choices.label: D
choices.text: The liver is an organ rich in donor immune cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocytes present alloantigens on MHC class II

explanation.summary: GVHD occurs most often with HSC transplants but can also follow transplants of organs rich in immune cells, such as the liver, or transfusion of non-irradiated blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that GVHD occurs most frequently with HSC transplants but may also occur in transplants of organs rich in immune cells, such as liver transplants, or a transfusion of non-irradiated blood. Immune cells from the graft recognize the recipient's tissue as foreign, producing the rash and diarrhea typical of GVHD affecting skin and GI tract.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both ABO and MHC matching influence transplant outcomes; matching requirements do not explain the presence of attacking donor lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC class I on graft cells is what recipient CTLs attack in rejection; it does not explain donor cells attacking the recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrotic bile ducts are a feature of chronic rejection years later, not a source of donor lymphocytes at three weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatocytes presenting alloantigen would drive rejection by recipient T cells, not GVHD by donor lymphocytes.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A premature neonate in the intensive care unit requires a red blood cell transfusion. The blood bank gamma-irradiates the unit before release. Which of the following best describes how irradiation prevents the complication being avoided?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radiation inactivates preformed isoagglutinins in donor plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiation strips ABO antigens from the donor red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electrons damage lymphocyte DNA so donor lymphocytes cannot proliferate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radiation denatures donor MHC molecules so recipient T cells cannot recognize them

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiation depletes donor complement so C1 cannot bind IgG

explanation.summary: Gamma-irradiation prevents transfusion-associated GVHD by generating electrons that damage lymphocyte DNA, rendering donor lymphocytes unable to proliferate and engraft.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that gamma-irradiation is performed to prevent transfusion-associated GVHD, a rare and usually fatal complication caused by infusion of viable lymphocytes that engraft in the recipient and mount an immune response. Irradiation generates electrons that damage lymphocyte DNA, rendering the lymphocytes unable to proliferate. People who need irradiated blood include neonates and immunocompromised people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isoagglutinins are antibodies in plasma; the purpose of irradiation is to disable donor lymphocytes, not antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ABO antigens are handled by blood-group matching; irradiation targets lymphocyte DNA, not red cell antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irradiation does not act by altering MHC molecules; it prevents donor lymphocytes from proliferating after infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complement is not the target of irradiation, and transfusion-associated GVHD is a lymphocyte-mediated, not complement-mediated, process.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with acute leukemia undergoes total body irradiation and chemotherapy before an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Which of the following best describes how this conditioning contributes to the afferent phase of graft-versus-host disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conditioning triggers preformed recipient antibodies, which bind and destroy donor stem cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiation damages the DNA of donor lymphocytes, so the graft's T cells cannot proliferate in the host

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conditioning eliminates recipient antigen-presenting cells, so donor T cells never encounter host alloantigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chemotherapy induces recipient regulatory T cells, which suppress donor CTLs and NK cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue damage raises inflammatory cytokines and MHC expression, enhancing alloantigen presentation

explanation.summary: In the afferent phase of GVHD, pre-transplant radiation or chemotherapy damages recipient tissue, increasing inflammatory cytokines and MHC antigen expression and enhancing APC presentation of alloantigens to donor T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick divides GVHD pathogenesis into three phases. In the afferent phase, radiation or chemotherapy before bone marrow transplantation damages recipient tissue, leading to increased levels of inflammatory cytokines and expression of MHC antigens; this enhances the APC's ability to present alloantigens to the donor T cells. This is followed by the efferent phase (donor T cell interaction with host APC) and effector phase (CTL and NK cell migration to target organs).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Preformed recipient antibodies mediate hyperacute rejection of solid organs; GVHD is driven by donor T cells attacking recipient tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiation damaging donor lymphocyte DNA describes gamma-irradiation of blood products to prevent transfusion-associated GVHD; conditioning targets the recipient, not the graft.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conditioning enhances rather than eliminates alloantigen presentation; the efferent phase depends on donor T cells interacting with host APCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe conditioning inducing regulatory T cells; it describes increased inflammatory cytokines that promote GVHD.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with leukemia receives an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant and develops mild graft-versus-host disease. Her oncologist notes that this complication may reduce her risk of leukemia relapse. Which of the following best explains this potential benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor immune cells reject the recipient's cancerous cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recipient CTLs are activated by the donor graft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunosuppressive drugs used for GVHD kill leukemic cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammatory cytokines induce telomerase in leukemic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Donor isoagglutinins agglutinate circulating leukemic cells

explanation.summary: GVHD can be beneficial when the donor immune system rejects the recipient's cancerous cells, called the graft-versus-tumor effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that GVHD might actually be beneficial in rare cases: GVHD causes rejection of cancerous cells by the donor immune system, known as the graft-versus-tumor effect. The same donor immune cells that attack recipient tissues can also attack residual leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The recipient's immune cells were eliminated by conditioning; GVHD and the graft-versus-tumor effect are mediated by donor, not recipient, cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppressive drugs prevent and treat GVHD by inhibiting lymphocytes; they are not described as killing leukemic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Telomerase expression promotes cancer cell survival by halting telomere shortening; inducing it would not reduce relapse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isoagglutinins are ABO antibodies that agglutinate mismatched red blood cells; they play no role in the graft-versus-tumor effect.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was treated for myeloid leukemia with chemotherapy followed by an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant from an unrelated donor 9 years ago. She now presents with a new myeloproliferative neoplasm. Genetic sequencing shows that all malignant cells carry the donor's genotype rather than her own. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her original leukemic clone acquired donor MHC alleles through antigenic modulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor HSCs engrafted, and a cancer later developed within the donor-derived cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Graft-versus-host disease transformed her own hematopoietic cells into a neoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residual recipient cells outcompeted the donor graft and then became malignant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preformed recipient antibodies caused hyperacute rejection of the donor stem cells

explanation.summary: When a post-transplant neoplasm is entirely of donor genotype, the donor HSCs must have engrafted and the cancer developed within donor cells that neither immune system eliminated.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case connection reasons that because the second leukemia consisted solely of donor cells, the donor HSCs must have successfully engrafted. The recipient's own immune cells were killed by chemotherapy or radiation before transplant, so her immune system was either eliminated or unable to outcompete the donor cells. At some point cancer developed within donor cells, and neither the patient's inborn immune system nor the engrafted immune system was able to eliminate it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigenic modulation is selection of tumor cells expressing less antigen under ADCC pressure; it does not change a cell's genotype to the donor's.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GVHD is donor immune cells damaging recipient skin, liver, and GI tract; it would not produce malignant cells of donor genotype from her own cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: If recipient cells had outcompeted the graft, the neoplasm would carry her genotype, not the donor's.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperacute rejection of the graft would have prevented engraftment, yet the malignant cells are donor-derived, proving the graft engrafted.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A tumor sequencing report describes a point mutation in a gene that normally regulates cell division; the mutated gene now drives uncontrolled proliferation and cancer. Before it was mutated, which of the following terms best describes this gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Telomerase gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oncogene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neoantigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proto-oncogene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oncogenic viral gene

explanation.summary: A proto-oncogene regulates normal cell division; once mutated so that it causes cancer, it is called an oncogene.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that oncogenes are mutated genes that cause cancer, and that before an oncogene becomes mutated it is called a proto-oncogene, which plays a role in regulating normal cell division. The unmutated regulator of cell division in this report is therefore a proto-oncogene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Telomerase is an aberrantly expressed self-protein in most cancers that halts telomere shortening; it is not the regulator of cell division described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oncogene is the term for the gene after it has mutated and causes cancer, not before.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A neoantigen is a new antigen within a mutated self-protein that differs substantially from normal; it is a protein feature, not the gene's pre-mutation name.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oncogenic viral proteins come from viruses such as HPV; this gene is the patient's own.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte recognizes a neoantigen presented on class I MHC by a melanoma cell. Through which of the following does the CTL induce apoptosis of the cancer cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgG binding to Fc receptors with ADCC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Assembly of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perforin and granzymes or Fas-FasL interactions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of TGF-beta and IL-10

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactive oxygen species from recruited neutrophils

explanation.summary: When a neoantigen is presented on class I MHC, CTLs induce apoptosis of the cancer cell via perforin and granzymes or Fas-FasL interactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that when a neoantigen is expressed and can be presented by class I MHC, CTLs can respond and induce apoptosis in the cancer cell via perforin and granzymes or Fas-FasL interactions. The brick's figure shows the CD8+ T cell delivering perforin and granzymes to the cancer cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADCC involves antibody-bound cells being killed by cells bearing Fc receptors such as NK cells, not TCR-mediated CTL killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The membrane attack complex is a complement product that punches holes in membranes during hyperacute rejection; CTLs do not assemble complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta and IL-10 are immunosuppressive cytokines that tumors use to blunt Th1 and M1 responses, not CTL killing mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive oxygen species from neutrophils are part of Fc-mediated inflammation in hyperacute rejection, not the CTL apoptosis pathway.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A tumor carries mutations that do not produce peptides compatible with the peptide-binding groove of class I MHC. In the resulting innate response, NK cells release IFN-gamma, which acts on macrophages; the macrophages then release a cytokine that activates the NK cells to kill the tumor with perforin and granzymes. Which of the following is the macrophage-derived cytokine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C5a

choices.label: B
choices.text: IFN-gamma

choices.label: C
choices.text: TGF-beta

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-10

choices.label: E
choices.text: IL-12

explanation.summary: In the NK cell response to tumors with poor MHC I presentation, NK-derived IFN-gamma stimulates macrophages to release IL-12, which activates NK cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that when tumor-associated antigens cannot be presented by MHC I, for example when changes do not yield peptides compatible with the peptide-binding groove, NK cells make up the dominant immune response. The brick's figure of this response shows the NK cell releasing IFN-gamma onto a macrophage, the macrophage releasing IL-12, and IL-12 driving activation of NK cells, which then kill the cancer cell with perforin and granzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C5a is a complement fragment that attracts and activates neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils in hyperacute rejection, not a macrophage cytokine in the anti-tumor loop.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-gamma is the cytokine released by the NK cell to stimulate the macrophage, not the macrophage's reply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TGF-beta is a tumor-derived suppressive cytokine that decreases activating receptors on NK cells rather than activating them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is a suppressive cytokine that induces M2 macrophages and regulatory T cells; it does not activate NK cells.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A carcinoma downregulates its co-stimulatory molecules. Antigen-presenting cells take up shed tumor antigens and present them to naive T cells without providing co-stimulation. Which of the following is the most likely outcome for the tumor-specific T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance to the tumor antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Differentiation into Th1 cells that recruit macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selection of antigen-loss tumor variants through ADCC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activation of NK cells through stress-associated signals

choices.label: E
choices.text: Generation of memory cells that accelerate tumor rejection

explanation.summary: In the absence of co-stimulatory molecules, presented tumor self-peptides induce T cell peripheral tolerance, allowing the tumor to be treated as a tolerogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists tolerance as a tumor evasion strategy: in the absence of co-stimulatory molecules, any presented self-peptides may induce T cell peripheral tolerance. Its figure shows that without co-stimulation, tumor antigens are taken up and presented by APCs to tolerize T cells, so the tumor is treated as a self antigen (tolerogen).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Th1 differentiation requires proper activation; presentation without co-stimulation tolerizes rather than activates T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selection of antigen-loss variants is antigenic modulation driven by antibody and ADCC, a separate evasion strategy not involving T cell co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cell activation by stress signals is independent of T cell antigen presentation and is not the consequence of missing co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Memory generation follows productive activation; tolerized T cells do not form memory that accelerates rejection.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with lymphoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody against a surface antigen on her tumor cells; the antibody kills tumor cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Months later the lymphoma relapses, and the relapsed cells no longer express the targeted antigen. Which tumor evasion strategy does this best illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low immunogenicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigenic modulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of peripheral tolerance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor-induced immune suppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Creation of an immune-privileged site

explanation.summary: Antigenic modulation occurs when antibody binding and ADCC select for cancer cells that present less of the targeted tumor-associated antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines antigenic modulation: if antibodies bind tumor antigens and mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, cancer cells that present less tumor-associated antigen are selected for. Its figure describes antibody against tumor cell-surface antigens inducing endocytosis and degradation of the antigen and immune selection of antigen-loss variants, exactly what the antigen-negative relapse shows.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low immunogenicity refers to downregulating class I MHC, adhesion molecules, or co-stimulatory molecules, not loss of a specific antibody-targeted antigen under ADCC pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral tolerance results from presenting antigen without co-stimulation; it does not involve antibody-driven selection of antigen-loss variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune suppression uses TGF-beta and IL-10 to induce Tregs and M2 macrophages; the tumor here escaped by losing the antigen, not by suppressing effectors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune privilege involves extracellular matrix barriers and PD-L1 upregulation, neither of which is described in this relapse.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A hepatocellular carcinoma re-expresses a protein that is normally produced only during fetal life and is essentially absent from adult tissues. Although the protein is unmutated, cytotoxic T lymphocytes are found to recognize and kill the tumor cells presenting it. Which of the following best explains why CTLs can respond to this self-protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is presented on class II MHC rather than class I

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is encoded by an oncogenic virus whose genome is integrated in the tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contains a neoantigen generated by a point mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its normal expression is so limited that CTLs can recognize it

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is coated by surface IgG that triggers NK cell killing

explanation.summary: Some aberrantly expressed self-proteins, such as fetal proteins, have such limited normal expression that CTLs can recognize them on tumor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that some aberrantly-expressed self-proteins, such as fetal proteins, have such limited expression that CTLs can recognize them. Because the fetal protein is presented in class I MHC on the tumor and is essentially absent elsewhere in the adult, the CTL response proceeds even though the protein is unmutated self.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLs recognize peptides presented in class I MHC; presentation on class II would engage helper T cells, not CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem describes a normal fetal self-protein, not an oncogenic viral protein such as those of HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The protein is stated to be unmutated, so it does not contain a mutation-derived neoantigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surface-bound IgG recognized by NK cells is an antibody-dependent mechanism; the stem describes CTL recognition of a presented self-protein.

questions.topicName: Tumors and Transplants

questions.stem: A researcher studies blood cell formation in a human embryo at roughly 4 weeks after fertilization, well before the liver or bone marrow are functional. Which of the following structures is the primary source of hematopoietic stem cells at this earliest stage of development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yolk sac

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymus

explanation.summary: Hematopoiesis begins in the extraembryonic yolk sac before shifting to the fetal liver and finally the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Until roughly 2 months (about 8 weeks) post-fertilization, hematopoietic stem cells and the developing myeloid and lymphoid cells are made primarily by the yolk sac, an extraembryonic structure. Only later does blood formation move into the embryo proper.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The fetal liver becomes the dominant site later, from about weeks 10-24, not at 4 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The bone marrow does not become the primary hematopoietic site until roughly 7-8 months post-fertilization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen only makes a minor contribution during mid-gestation, not at the earliest stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus is the site of T-cell maturation and contributes only minimally to hematopoiesis, not at 4 weeks.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that some leukocytes in adults are continuously produced in the bone marrow, whereas others are long-lived tissue-resident populations seeded before birth. Which of the following cell types is generated exclusively from the bone marrow in an adult?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epidermal Langerhans cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mast cells

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are short-lived circulating cells made continuously in the marrow, unlike fetal-derived tissue-resident cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils are circulating cells that are not tissue-resident; they survive in tissues only a few days and must be replenished from bone marrow throughout life. Many tissue-resident populations, by contrast, originate at least in part from fetal sources and self-renew.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Microglia are macrophages derived exclusively from the fetus and self-renew without bone marrow input.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alveolar macrophages are tissue-resident cells derived at least in part from the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Langerhans cells are fetal-derived epidermal macrophage-like cells, not marrow-exclusive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cell populations are at least partially derived from the fetus.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A neuroscientist studying an older adult with progressive neurodegenerative disease focuses on a self-renewing, tissue-resident macrophage of the brain whose age-related dysfunction, driven by telomere shortening and oxidative stress, is linked to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. This cell is derived exclusively from the fetus. Which of the following cells is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Microglia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kupffer cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: B-1 cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages

explanation.summary: Microglia are fetal-derived CNS macrophages whose aging is tied to neurodegenerative disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microglia support and protect the central nervous system and are derived exclusively from the fetus. Aging affects microglia through telomere shortening, DNA damage, and oxidative stress, impairing self-renewal; this dysfunction is associated with cognitive decline and with Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Kupffer cells are liver macrophages of fetal origin that are gradually replaced by marrow-derived cells, not a CNS population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are short-lived circulating marrow-derived cells, not brain-resident macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B-1 cells are a fetal-derived B-lymphocyte subset that secretes low-affinity IgM, not CNS macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alveolar macrophages reside in the lung, not the brain.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: During a study of thymic development, an investigator traces the stromal framework of the thymus, including its cortical and medullary epithelial cells, back to a single embryologic structure. From which of the following does the thymic stroma arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Third pharyngeal pouch endoderm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neural crest ectoderm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yolk sac mesoderm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paraxial mesoderm (somites)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fetal liver endoderm

explanation.summary: The thymic stroma originates from endodermal cells of the ventral third pharyngeal pouch.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus originates during early gestation from endodermal cells of the ventral third pharyngeal pouch. Its stromal (supportive, non-hemopoietic) cells, including cortical and medullary thymic epithelial cells, fibroblasts, connective tissue cells, and endothelial cells, all arise from the third pharyngeal pouch.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes thymic stroma to third pharyngeal pouch endoderm, not neural crest ectoderm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The yolk sac is a hematopoietic source, not the origin of the thymic stromal framework.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somites are nascent body segments and do not give rise to the thymic stroma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Developing T cells are hematopoietic and invade the thymus; the fetal liver does not form the thymic stroma.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A full-term newborn is found to have serum IgG levels equivalent to those of an adult, despite never having mounted its own antibody response. Which of the following receptors is responsible for transporting this IgG from the parent to the fetus across the placenta?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fc-gamma receptor III (CD16)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complement receptor 1 (CR1)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mannose receptor

explanation.summary: Transplacental IgG transfer is mediated by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).
explanation.whyCorrect: During the prenatal period, the fetus acquires IgG by transplacental transport. The neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) binds IgG at the fetal-parent interface of the placenta and transcytoses it into the fetal circulation, so neonates are born with IgG levels equivalent to adults.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor transports IgA across mucosal epithelium (for example into breastmilk), not IgG across the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD16 mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells, not placental IgG transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement receptor 1 binds complement fragments, not IgG for transplacental transport.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mannose receptor is a pattern-recognition receptor for pathogen uptake, not an antibody-transport receptor.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 6-month-old formula-fed infant presents with several bacterial infections over a short period. The pediatrician notes this age corresponds to a recognized window of increased susceptibility. Which of the following best explains the vulnerability during this period?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maternal transplacental IgG has waned before the infant produces enough of its own

choices.label: B
choices.text: The infant has a congenital absence of the thymus and cannot make T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The neonatal Fc receptor is defective and cannot bind IgG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal IgG continues to rise and suppresses the infant's own antibody production

choices.label: E
choices.text: The infant permanently lacks the ability to class-switch to IgG

explanation.summary: Between 3 and 12 months, a 'danger zone' occurs as maternal IgG wanes before the infant's own IgG is fully generated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Between 3 and 12 months after birth, transplacental (maternal) IgG wanes in the blood while the child has not yet generated much of its own immunoglobulin. This transient trough in humoral immunity leaves the infant more susceptible to infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrent infection at this age reflects the normal antibody 'danger zone,' not congenital athymia; nothing suggests a T-cell developmental defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcRn functions normally; neonates are in fact born with adult-equivalent IgG because of it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal IgG is waning, not rising, during this window, and it does not suppress the infant's own production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The infant is beginning to make its own immunoglobulin; there is no permanent class-switching defect implied.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A lactation researcher studies how secretory IgA reaches breastmilk. IgA is produced by plasma cells in the lamina propria of the mammary glands and must cross the alveolar epithelium to enter the milk. Which of the following mediates this transport across the mammary epithelium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)

choices.label: C
choices.text: J chain acting alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fc-epsilon receptor I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toll-like receptor 4

explanation.summary: Secretory IgA is transported across the mammary epithelium into breastmilk by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: sIgA is generated from plasma cells in the lamina propria of the mammary glands and is then transported across the mammary alveolar epithelium into breastmilk by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR). This sIgA coats the infant's mucosal surfaces.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FcRn transports IgG (for example across the placenta), not IgA across mammary epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The J chain joins IgA monomers but does not by itself carry IgA across the epithelium; pIgR performs the transcytosis.
