whyWrongByChoice.D: Fc-epsilon receptor I binds IgE on mast cells and basophils, not IgA for secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR4 is a pattern-recognition receptor for LPS and does not transport antibody into milk.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A breastfed neonate's gut is protected in part by cells present in breastmilk that engulf secretory IgA and then release it upon contact with bacteria in the intestinal lumen. These cells make up the majority of the immune cells in breastmilk. Which of the following components is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactoferrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysozyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lymphocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oligosaccharides

explanation.summary: Breastmilk macrophages carry engulfed sIgA and release it onto bacteria in the infant gut.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breastmilk contains up to about 1 million immune cells per milliliter, and the majority (55-60%) are macrophages. These breastmilk macrophages contain engulfed sIgA that they release upon contact with bacteria in the lumen of the infant gut.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactoferrin competes for ferric iron to inhibit bacterial growth; it does not carry and release sIgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme cleaves peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls and is not a cell that transports sIgA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Breastmilk lymphocytes are predominantly T cells that express cytokines; they are a minority (5-10%) of milk cells and are not the sIgA-releasing population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oligosaccharides are prebiotic carbohydrates that feed beneficial gut microbiota, not cells that deliver sIgA.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A pediatric researcher characterizes a breastmilk protein that limits bacterial growth in the infant gut by binding and sequestering ferric iron so that bacteria cannot use it. Which of the following breastmilk components has this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lactoferrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysozyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oligosaccharides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defensins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory IgA

explanation.summary: Lactoferrin inhibits bacterial growth by competing for ferric iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactoferrin is a breastmilk protein that competes for ferric iron and thereby inhibits bacterial growth. By sequestering the iron that bacteria need, it starves them of an essential nutrient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme cleaves peptidoglycans in bacterial cell walls rather than binding iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oligosaccharides are prebiotics that feed beneficial gut bacteria such as Bifidobacteria and block pathogen binding, not iron chelators.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defensins are small molecules that disrupt viral envelopes and target bacteria and viruses, not iron-binding proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretory IgA coats mucosal surfaces in a non-inflammatory way; it does not sequester iron.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: Four days after birth, an infant delivered by Cesarean section is evaluated for its establishing skin microbiome. Because the infant did not pass through the birth canal, its skin flora is being shaped largely by close skin-to-skin contact. The infant's skin microbiome would most closely resemble which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The skin flora of the primary parent or caregiver

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vaginal flora of the person who birthed the infant

choices.label: C
choices.text: The intestinal flora of an older sibling

choices.label: D
choices.text: The skin flora of the obstetrician

choices.label: E
choices.text: The oral flora of a grandparent who visits on day three

explanation.summary: A C-section infant's skin flora most resembles the skin flora of whoever spends the most time in skin-to-skin contact, usually the primary caregiver.
explanation.whyCorrect: This individual almost certainly spends the most time in skin-to-skin contact with the infant, so their skin microbes seed the newborn's skin. Providing the greatest chance of microbial transfer, the primary parent or caregiver's skin flora is the best match.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaginal flora would be relevant to a vaginal delivery, not a Cesarean section, where that exposure is minimal to absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An older sibling would only contribute if in close contact, and intestinal flora is not the skin source acquired through skin-to-skin contact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Good hospital staff practices, such as wearing gloves, make transfer of significant microbes from the obstetrician unlikely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A grandparent visiting once on day three contributes far less than the caregiver in constant skin-to-skin contact, and oral flora is not the skin source.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with recurrent, severe lower respiratory infections including pneumonia. You order a CBC with differential, a lymphocyte-subset panel, and a chest X-ray. Which of the following results should be considered abnormal rather than an expected age-related change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: White blood cell count of 25,000 cells/mm^3

choices.label: B
choices.text: A small amount of vestigial thymus, not visible on chest X-ray

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absence of a visible thymus on chest X-ray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced CD4+/CD8+ ratio relative to a young adult

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced naive B cells relative to a young adult

explanation.summary: A WBC of 25,000 is above the adult normal range and is abnormal, whereas thymic involution and reduced naive T/B cells are expected with age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal adult WBC counts are 4000-11,000 cells/mm^3, so 25,000 cells/mm^3 is clearly elevated and abnormal. The other findings reflect normal aging.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Age-related thymic hypoplasia is normal in adults; a vestigial thymus that cannot be seen on chest X-ray is expected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absence of a visible thymus on chest X-ray reflects normal age-related thymic regression, not disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A reduced CD4+/CD8+ ratio relative to a young adult is a recognized age-related change.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced naive B-cell production relative to a young adult is expected with immunosenescence.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman is being counseled about why her immune function has changed with age. Her physician explains that age-related regression of the thymus alters the circulating T-cell pool. Which of the following changes is most consistent with this thymic involution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased production of naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased output of naive T cells from an enlarging thymus

choices.label: C
choices.text: An increased CD4+/CD8+ ratio compared with a young adult

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced antibody affinity and reduced autoantibody levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Improved class-switching and expanded naive B-cell production

explanation.summary: Thymic involution reduces naive CD4+/CD8+ T-cell output and shifts the T-cell pool toward memory and effector cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In late life, age-related regression of the thymus alters the circulating T-cell pool: production of naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells declines, while the percentages of memory T cells and non-proliferative effector T cells increase. Additional changes include a decreased CD4+/CD8+ ratio and skewing toward Th17 and regulatory T-cell subsets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The aging thymus involutes and its output declines; it does not enlarge or increase naive T-cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aging is associated with a decreased, not increased, CD4+/CD8+ ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.D: With age, general antibody affinity declines while autoantibody levels increase, the opposite of this choice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class-switching becomes impaired and naive B-cell production declines with age, not improves.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A fetus at 16 weeks post fertilization is evaluated during a research study of blood cell production. Which of the following is the primary site of hematopoiesis at this stage of development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yolk sac

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymus

explanation.summary: From weeks 10-24 post fertilization, the liver is the primary site of hematopoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In weeks 10-24, hematopoiesis primarily occurs in the fetal liver, with some contribution from the spleen, thymus, and bone marrow. A 16-week fetus therefore falls squarely in the hepatic phase of blood cell production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The yolk sac is the primary source of hematopoietic stem cells only until roughly 2 months (about 8 weeks) post fertilization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The bone marrow is seeded by liver-derived HSCs at about 12 weeks but does not become the primary site until 7-8 months post fertilization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen makes only a minor contribution during mid-gestation and is never the primary site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus contributes only minimally to hematopoiesis; it is the site of T-cell maturation.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A healthy 32-year-old man volunteers as a hematopoietic stem cell donor. During bone marrow harvesting, the healthcare team uses large hollow needles to aspirate marrow. From which of the following sites is the marrow most likely obtained?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pelvic bones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sternum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skull

choices.label: D
choices.text: Femoral shaft

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertebrae

explanation.summary: Donor HSCs are harvested by pulling bone marrow from the pelvic bones with large hollow needles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow harvesting is the procedure used to obtain donor HSCs for HSC transplant. Providers use large hollow needles that pull bone marrow from the donor's pelvic bones, one of the few sites where hematopoiesis still occurs in adults.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The sternum is an adult hematopoietic site, but it is not the site described for bone marrow harvesting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The skull contains hematopoietic marrow in adults, but marrow is not harvested from it for transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In adults, hematopoietic marrow is limited to the skull, sternum, vertebrae, and pelvic bones; the femoral shaft is not among these sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vertebrae are an adult hematopoietic site, but harvesting for transplant uses the pelvic bones.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A researcher uses lineage tracing to follow the origin of liver Kupffer cells from fetal life into adulthood and compares the result with brain microglia. Which of the following best describes the origin of Kupffer cells across the lifespan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal in origin at first, gradually replaced by bone-marrow-derived cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal in origin throughout life, never replenished by bone-marrow-derived cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow in origin from birth, with no fetal contribution at any stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Third pharyngeal pouch in origin, persisting as a non-hematopoietic stroma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Circulating neutrophils in origin, replenished every few days from the marrow

explanation.summary: Kupffer cells begin as fetal-derived tissue-resident macrophages but are gradually replaced by bone-marrow-derived cells over life.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some initially tissue-resident macrophage populations, such as liver Kupffer cells, are of fetal origin but are gradually replaced with bone-marrow-derived cells over a person's life. This contrasts with microglia and brain-resident mast cells, which are not replenished by bone-marrow-derived cells at all and instead self-renew.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lifelong fetal origin without marrow replenishment describes microglia and brain-resident mast cells, not Kupffer cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kupffer cells are initially of fetal origin; they are not exclusively marrow-derived from birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to thymic stroma, not to liver macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kupffer cells are macrophages, not neutrophils, and neutrophils are the short-lived circulating population, not a tissue-resident one.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: An immunologist studies a lymphoid population in adult peripheral tissues that is derived from fetal tissues, functions without T-cell help, and secretes antibodies of limited specificity. Which of the following cell types is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B-1 cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tissue-resident NK cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regulatory T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Langerhans cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mast cells

explanation.summary: B-1 cells are fetal-derived B cells that secrete limited-specificity antibody in a T-cell-independent manner.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some subsets of lymphoid cells are derived from fetal tissues. One subset is B-1 cells, B cells that function in a T-cell-independent manner, secreting antibodies with limited specificity in peripheral tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tissue-resident NK cells also first emerge independent of bone marrow HSCs, but they do not secrete antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regulatory T cells are T lymphocytes and do not secrete antibody; the described population is T-cell independent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Langerhans cells are fetal-derived epidermal macrophages, not antibody-secreting lymphoid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cells are fetal-derived tissue-resident cells but are myeloid, not antibody-secreting lymphoid cells.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: At 9-10 weeks post fertilization, prothymocytes invade the developing thymus, proliferate, and help differentiate the cortex and medulla. Which of the following is the source of these hematopoietic cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yolk sac

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Third pharyngeal pouch endoderm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spleen

explanation.summary: Thymocytes invade the thymus from the fetal liver, the source of hematopoietic stem cells at weeks 9-10.
explanation.whyCorrect: Developing T cells are hematopoietic, unlike the thymic stroma. At 9-10 weeks post fertilization, prothymocytes invade the thymus from the fetal liver, which is the site of hematopoiesis during weeks 10-24. Vascularization follows in the next few weeks, with subsequent migration of dendritic cells and macrophages into the thymus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The yolk sac phase of hematopoiesis ends at roughly 8 weeks, before prothymocytes seed the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The bone marrow is only being seeded at about 12 weeks and does not become the primary hematopoietic site until 7-8 months.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the non-hemopoietic thymic stroma, not to thymocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen makes only a minor contribution to hematopoiesis during mid-gestation and is not the source of thymocytes.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: Histologic examination of a 20-week fetal thymus shows rounded groups of thymic epithelial cells that are unique to the medulla and first appeared around week 16 of development. Which of the following is the most likely function of these structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Regulation of dendritic cells and differentiation of regulatory T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive selection of thymocytes on cortical epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vascularization of the thymus during early gestation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generation of hematopoietic stem cells to seed the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formation of the fibroblast and connective tissue framework

explanation.summary: Hassall's corpuscles are medullary groups of TECs that appear to regulate dendritic cells and regulatory T-cell differentiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hassall's corpuscles are rounded groups of thymic epithelial cells unique to the thymic medulla that develop in week 16. These corpuscles appear to function in the regulation of dendritic cells and the differentiation of regulatory T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Positive selection is a function of the thymic cortex, whereas these structures are unique to the medulla.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vascularization occurs in the weeks after prothymocytes invade and is not a function of Hassall's corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymic stroma is not hemopoietic; HSCs are generated by the yolk sac, liver, and marrow, not by thymic epithelial structures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibroblasts and connective tissue cells are separate stromal components derived from the third pharyngeal pouch, not the function of Hassall's corpuscles.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A mother who is unable to breastfeed her 2-week-old infant is worried that formula feeding will leave the baby defenseless against infection. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling point about the infant's immune protection at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transplacental IgG acquired before birth still provides passive protection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secretory IgA delivered by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor is still present

choices.label: C
choices.text: Germinal centers in the intestinal Peyer's patches already generate antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactoferrin in the infant gut continues to sequester ferric iron from bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Milk macrophages continue to release engulfed sIgA onto luminal bacteria

explanation.summary: A formula-fed infant still has transplacental IgG and a developing mucosal immune system, so 'fed is best' rather than 'breast is best.'
explanation.whyCorrect: Many other portions of the infant's immune system can aid in defense against pathogens, such as transplacental IgG and the developing mucosal immune system. Transplacental IgG, transported by FcRn before birth, is present at adult-equivalent levels at birth and only wanes over the following months. The infant may have more mucosal infections than a breastfed child, but exposure to pathogens and sanitation affect infection rates as well, and proper caloric intake is vital for growth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Secretory IgA transported by pIgR is a breastmilk component and is not supplied to a formula-fed infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Germinal centers and activated lymphocytes are found in the intestinal mucosa only after weaning; neonatal Peyer's patch lymphocytes remain naive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactoferrin is a breastmilk protein; it is not available to a formula-fed infant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Breastmilk macrophages carrying engulfed sIgA are delivered only through breastmilk.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A sample of human breastmilk is analyzed and found to contain nearly 1 million immune cells per milliliter. After macrophages, which of the following is the next most abundant immune cell type in breastmilk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: T lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: B lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eosinophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mast cells

explanation.summary: Breastmilk immune cells are mostly macrophages (55-60%), followed by neutrophils (30-40%) and lymphocytes (5-10%).
explanation.whyCorrect: Breastmilk contains up to 1 million immune cells per milliliter. The majority (55-60%) are macrophages, but neutrophils (30-40%) and lymphocytes (5-10%) are also present, making neutrophils the second most abundant population.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocytes make up only 5-10% of breastmilk immune cells; although they are predominantly T cells, they are far fewer than neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B lymphocytes are a minority of the already small lymphocyte fraction, which is predominantly T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eosinophils are not described as a major cellular component of breastmilk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cells are not described as a major cellular component of breastmilk.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 5-month-old exclusively breastfed infant is beginning to be introduced to solid foods. The pediatrician notes that breastmilk cytokines are thought to be important for the infant's development of tolerance to ingested antigens. Which of the following breastmilk cytokines has this role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: TGF-beta

choices.label: B
choices.text: TNF-alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL-6

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perforin

explanation.summary: Breastmilk TGF-beta and IL-10 are thought to promote infant tolerance to ingested antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many cytokines can be found in breastmilk. Some, like TGF-beta and IL-10, are thought to be important for infant development of tolerance to ingested antigens. Together with mucosal antigens passed in milk (bound to IgA or trafficked by immune cells), these anti-inflammatory cytokines support the generation of tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine, the type that aged dendritic cells and macrophages overproduce; it is not the tolerance-promoting breastmilk cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine, not the anti-inflammatory signal associated with oral tolerance in breastmilk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine and is not described as promoting tolerance to ingested antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is a cytotoxic molecule produced by CD8+ and NK cells, not a tolerance-promoting cytokine in breastmilk.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A breastmilk enzyme is found to cleave the peptidoglycan in the cell walls of bacteria in the infant gut. Which of the following breastmilk components has this activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lysozyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactoferrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defensins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oligosaccharides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory IgA

explanation.summary: Lysozyme is the breastmilk enzyme that cleaves bacterial cell wall peptidoglycans.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysozyme is an enzyme in human breastmilk that cleaves peptidoglycans in the cell walls of bacteria, providing direct antibacterial activity in the infant gut.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactoferrin competes for ferric iron to inhibit bacterial growth; it is not a peptidoglycan-cleaving enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defensins contain lipids that disrupt viral envelopes and glycosylated proteins that inhibit bacteria and viruses; they do not enzymatically cleave peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oligosaccharides are prebiotic carbohydrates that feed beneficial microbiota and block pathogen binding, not enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretory IgA coats mucosal surfaces in a non-inflammatory fashion; it has no enzymatic activity against cell walls.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: Stool analysis of a healthy exclusively breastfed 2-month-old infant shows a gut microbiota dominated by Bifidobacteria. Which of the following breastmilk components most directly promotes the growth of these beneficial bacteria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oligosaccharides

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactoferrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysozyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defensins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macrophages

explanation.summary: Breastmilk oligosaccharides are prebiotics that feed beneficial gut microbiota such as Bifidobacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oligosaccharides in breastmilk are carbohydrates that act as prebiotics; they feed infant beneficial gut microbiota such as Bifidobacteria. They also inhibit binding of pathogenic bacteria to the gut.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactoferrin inhibits bacterial growth by competing for ferric iron; it does not feed beneficial bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme cleaves bacterial peptidoglycan and is antibacterial rather than prebiotic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defensins disrupt viral envelopes and inhibit bacteria and viruses; they do not nourish the microbiota.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Breastmilk macrophages carry and release sIgA onto luminal bacteria; they are not a nutrient source for Bifidobacteria.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A class of small molecules in breastmilk contains lipids that disrupt viral envelopes as well as glycosylated proteins that inhibit both bacteria and viruses. Which of the following breastmilk components is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defensins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysozyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactoferrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oligosaccharides

choices.label: E
choices.text: TGF-beta

explanation.summary: Breastmilk defensins are small molecules with envelope-disrupting lipids and antimicrobial glycosylated proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Defensins are a class of small molecules in breastmilk. This class contains lipids that disrupt viral envelopes and glycosylated proteins that inhibit bacteria and viruses, giving them activity against both types of pathogen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme is a single enzyme that cleaves bacterial peptidoglycan; it has no described antiviral lipid component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin is a protein that competes for ferric iron to limit bacterial growth; it does not disrupt viral envelopes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oligosaccharides are prebiotic carbohydrates that feed beneficial bacteria and block pathogen binding, not antiviral lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is a cytokine associated with tolerance to ingested antigens, not a direct antimicrobial molecule.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: The mother of a healthy 4-month-old asks how long she should breastfeed and when it is appropriate to add other sources of nutrition. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which of the following is the recommended approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breastmilk exclusively until 6 months, with continued breastfeeding until 1 year

choices.label: B
choices.text: Breastmilk exclusively until 3 months, with continued breastfeeding until 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Breastmilk exclusively until 12 months, with continued breastfeeding until 2 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Breastmilk exclusively until 1 month, with continued breastfeeding until 6 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Breastmilk exclusively until 9 months, with continued breastfeeding until 18 months

explanation.summary: The AAP recommends exclusive breastmilk until 6 months and continued breastfeeding until one year of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Research suggests breastfed infants are less likely to develop ear infections, allergies, and gastrointestinal infections. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends breast milk as the exclusive nutrition for infants until 6 months, with continued breast feeding until one year of age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Three months of exclusive breastfeeding and stopping at 6 months falls short of the AAP recommendation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exclusive breastmilk for the full first year and continued feeding to 2 years exceeds the stated recommendation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: One month of exclusive breastmilk is far shorter than the 6-month recommendation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nine months exclusive and 18 months total do not match the recommended 6-month and 1-year milestones.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term neonate is evaluated for vulnerability to mucosal infection. Compared with the adult small intestine, the neonatal intestine completely lacks a cell type that serves as a major source of antimicrobial substances in adult tissue. Which of the following cell types is absent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paneth cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Goblet cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enterocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dendritic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Naive T cells

explanation.summary: Neonatal intestines lack Paneth cells, a major source of antimicrobial substances in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immediately after birth, neonatal intestines lack Paneth cells, which are a major source of antimicrobial substances in the adult tissue. This absence, along with an unestablished normal flora, contributes to neonatal vulnerability to mucosal infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Goblet cells are present in the neonate; they simply make little mucus compared with those in an adult.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterocytes line the neonatal intestinal epithelium and are not absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dendritic cells are part of the neonatal Peyer's patch and are present at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T cells begin to populate the intestine immediately after birth, found in Peyer's patches, where they remain naive.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 10-day-old exclusively breastfed neonate is being evaluated in a study of the developing gut immune system. Which of the following best describes the intestinal lymphoid compartment at this pre-weaning stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: T and B cells are found only in Peyer's patches and remain naive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germinal centers with activated lymphocytes fill the lamina propria

choices.label: C
choices.text: M cells have been abundant since birth and deliver antigen to Peyer's patches

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paneth cells supply the majority of the mucosal antimicrobial substances

choices.label: E
choices.text: Goblet cells produce mucus in amounts comparable to those of an adult

explanation.summary: Before weaning, intestinal T and B cells are confined to Peyer's patches and stay naive; germinal centers appear only after weaning.
explanation.whyCorrect: T and B cells begin to populate the intestine immediately after birth, but they are only found in Peyer's patches and remain naive throughout the neonatal phase. Germinal centers and activated lymphocytes can only be found in the intestinal mucosa after weaning.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Germinal centers and activated lymphocytes are found in the intestinal mucosa only after weaning, not at 10 days of life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M cells are not initially present at birth; they can be seen only after the second week after birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neonatal intestines lack Paneth cells, so they cannot supply antimicrobial substances at this age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neonatal goblet cells are present but make little mucus compared with those in an adult.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant born in the United States has stool testing that shows no detectable Bifidobacteria, a finding present in roughly 25% of infants in the country. The absence of this genus, considered the cornerstone of infant microbiome establishment, is most associated with an increased risk of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atopy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transient low IgG levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thymic hypoplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced CD4+/CD8+ ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired class-switching

explanation.summary: Bifidobacteria presence is associated with reduced risk of atopy, so its absence raises atopy risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotic use, lifestyle, sanitation and hygiene, and dietary habits have shifted the microbiome in industrialized society, and in the United States roughly 25% of infants lack detectable Bifidobacteria. This genus is the cornerstone of infant microbiome establishment, and its presence is associated with a reduced risk of atopy; the early microbiome may help prevent atopy and other non-inherited disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transient low IgG between 3 and 12 months results from waning transplacental IgG, not from the microbiome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic hypoplasia is a normal age-related change in adults and is unrelated to gut Bifidobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A reduced CD4+/CD8+ ratio is an age-related T-cell change of late life, not a consequence of the infant microbiome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired class-switching is a feature of immunosenescence in older adults, not of an infant lacking Bifidobacteria.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A term newborn is 12 hours old and appears well. A routine complete blood count shows a white blood cell count of 22,000 cells/mm^3. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Within the expected range for a newborn

choices.label: B
choices.text: Above the expected range for a newborn

choices.label: C
choices.text: Below the expected range for a newborn

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the expected range for an adult

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the expected range for a 2-year-old child

explanation.summary: Newborns normally have far more total WBCs (9,000-30,000 cells/mm^3) than adults (4,000-11,000 cells/mm^3).
explanation.whyCorrect: The total WBC count varies greatly from neonate to adolescent. Young children, particularly newborns, have many more total WBCs; the newborn range is 9,000-30,000 cells/mm^3, so 22,000 cells/mm^3 in a 12-hour-old is within expected limits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 22,000 cells/mm^3 is below the upper newborn limit of 30,000 cells/mm^3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 22,000 cells/mm^3 is well above the lower newborn limit of 9,000 cells/mm^3.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The adult range is 4,000-11,000 cells/mm^3; 22,000 would be abnormal for an adult, but this patient is a newborn.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Children under 2 years have a range of 6,200-17,000 cells/mm^3, so 22,000 would exceed the expected range for a 2-year-old.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A healthy 1-year-old girl has a CBC with differential drawn at a well-child visit. The differential shows 61% lymphocytes and 31% neutrophils. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expected for age, because young children have more lymphocytes than neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abnormal, because neutrophils should be 50-70% of WBCs at every age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Abnormal, because lymphocytes should fall to 20-40% by 6 months of age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expected only during the first 24 hours of life, when lymphocytes predominate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abnormal, because monocytes should be the predominant leukocyte in infancy

explanation.summary: Young children normally have more lymphocytes than neutrophils (about 60% of WBCs), the reverse of the adult differential.
explanation.whyCorrect: WBC differentials change throughout the lifespan. Adult WBCs are predominantly neutrophils (50-70%) followed by lymphocytes (20-40%), but young children typically have more lymphocytes than neutrophils, with lymphocytes making up about 60% of WBCs. A 1-year-old with 61% lymphocytes is therefore normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The neutrophil range of 50-70% applies to adults, not to young children, in whom lymphocytes predominate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphocytes remain around 60% of WBCs through early childhood; the 20-40% range is the adult value.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In the first 24 hours of life neutrophils actually predominate; lymphocyte predominance develops over the following weeks and persists through early childhood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monocytes are a minor population (2-9% in adults) and never predominate at any age.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: At autopsy, the thymus of a previously healthy 16-year-old is examined and found to be less pink and more yellow than that of a young child, with substantial adipose tissue infiltrating the gland. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expected adipose infiltration that begins around the time of puberty

choices.label: B
choices.text: Premature immunosenescence, normally seen only after age 65

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the third pharyngeal pouch to form thymic stroma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of Hassall's corpuscles from the thymic medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maximal thymic output, which peaks during adolescence

explanation.summary: Around puberty, adipose infiltrates the thymus, changing its gross appearance from pink to yellow as part of age-related involution.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus reaches its maximal output during early postnatal life and declines thereafter in size and output through age-related involution. Around the time of puberty, adipose can be seen infiltrating the tissue; this infiltration is substantial and changes the gross appearance of the thymus so that it becomes less pink and more yellow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosenescence refers to the immune decline of those older than 65; fatty thymic involution beginning at puberty is normal, not premature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of stromal formation would prevent thymic development altogether; it does not explain fatty infiltration of a formed gland.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hassall's corpuscles are medullary structures that regulate dendritic cells and Treg differentiation; their absence is not the cause of fatty change.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymic output is maximal in early postnatal life, not adolescence, and declines from then on.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has laboratory evidence of chronic low-grade inflammation without an identifiable infection. His physician attributes this to age-related changes in dendritic cells and macrophages. Which of the following cytokine patterns is most consistent with immunosenescence in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less IL-10, more TNF-alpha and IL-6

choices.label: B
choices.text: More IL-10, less TNF-alpha and IL-6

choices.label: C
choices.text: More IL-10, more TNF-alpha and IL-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Less IL-10, less TNF-alpha and IL-1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Less IL-6, more IL-10 and IL-1

explanation.summary: Aged dendritic cells and macrophages make less anti-inflammatory IL-10 and more pro-inflammatory TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: In late life, dendritic cells and macrophages produce less anti-inflammatory IL-10 and more pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1). This shift underlies the chronic low-grade inflammation associated with immunosenescence, which increases the risk of noncommunicable diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease, and autoimmune diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: More IL-10 with fewer pro-inflammatory cytokines is the opposite of the aging pattern and would not produce chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 production decreases, not increases, with age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pro-inflammatory TNF-alpha and IL-1 increase with age; they do not decrease alongside IL-10.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-6 increases and IL-10 decreases with age, the reverse of this pattern.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman has recurrent bacterial skin infections. Her absolute neutrophil count is within the adult reference range, so functional testing of her neutrophils is performed. Which of the following results is most consistent with normal age-related neutrophil changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased extracellular trap formation and decreased peroxide production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased extracellular trap formation and decreased phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased trafficking to tissues and normal phagocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased peroxide production and decreased trafficking to tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal extracellular trap formation and increased phagocytosis

explanation.summary: Aged neutrophils show declines in NET formation, peroxide production, phagocytosis, and trafficking.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the late-life changes that reduce the ability to fight infection, neutrophils show declines in the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, peroxide production, phagocytosis, and trafficking. A normal neutrophil count can therefore coexist with impaired neutrophil function in an older adult.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Extracellular trap formation declines rather than increases with age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trafficking declines with age, and phagocytosis is reduced rather than normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peroxide production declines with age; it does not increase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both extracellular trap formation and phagocytosis decline in aged neutrophils.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man undergoes bone marrow analysis as part of an aging study. Compared with a 25-year-old, which of the following changes in his hematopoietic stem cells is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased capacity to produce lymphoid progenitors, with a bias toward myeloid progenitors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased capacity to produce myeloid progenitors, with a bias toward lymphoid progenitors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased capacity to produce both lymphoid and myeloid progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replacement of marrow HSCs by self-renewing yolk-sac-derived progenitors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete loss of HSCs, with leukocytes supplied only by fetal-derived tissue-resident pools

explanation.summary: Aged HSCs lose lymphoid potential and become biased toward myeloid progenitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: In late life, HSCs have a decreased capacity to produce lymphoid progenitors and are biased toward myeloid progenitors. This contributes to the decline in naive B-cell production and the absolute B-cell count seen with immunosenescence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The aging bias runs toward myeloid, not lymphoid, progenitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aged HSCs do not gain capacity; lymphoid output specifically declines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Yolk-sac-derived progenitors seed certain tissue-resident populations during fetal life; they do not replace adult marrow HSCs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The bone marrow produces leukocytes throughout the rest of a person's life; HSCs are not lost entirely, and neutrophils in particular require continuous marrow output.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with no symptoms of autoimmune disease is found to have low-titer serum autoantibodies on screening. Her physician explains that this reflects an expected age-related change in humoral immunity. Which of the following best describes antibody changes in late life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased general antibody affinity with increased autoantibody levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased general antibody affinity with increased autoantibody levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased general antibody affinity with decreased autoantibody levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased general antibody affinity with decreased autoantibody levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged general antibody affinity with decreased autoantibody levels

explanation.summary: With aging, general antibody affinity declines while autoantibody levels rise.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the B-cell changes of late life, general antibody affinity declines, but levels of autoantibodies increase. This accompanies a decline in the absolute B-cell count, reduced naive B-cell production, and impaired class-switching, and it fits with the increased risk of autoimmune disease associated with immunosenescence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody affinity declines rather than increases with age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both directions are wrong: affinity falls and autoantibodies rise in late life.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoantibody levels increase with age rather than decrease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Affinity is not unchanged; it declines, and autoantibodies increase rather than decrease.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System

questions.stem: An 85-year-old man has a poor antibody response to a routine vaccination. Flow cytometry of his T cells is compared with that of a young adult. Which of the following pairs of surface molecules is most likely to show decreased expression on his T cells as a result of aging?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3 and CD28

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 and CD25

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD16 and CD56

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD19 and CD21

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD80 and CD86

explanation.summary: Aging T cells lose expression of CD3 (TCR signaling) and CD28 (co-stimulation), impairing activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In late life, expression of CD3, which is important for TCR signaling, and CD28, a co-stimulatory molecule, decreases on T cells. Together with the loss of naive T cells from thymic involution, this contributes to the reduced response to vaccinations seen in immunosenescence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes a decreased CD4+/CD8+ ratio and skewing toward regulatory T cells with age, not loss of CD4 and CD25 from T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD16 and CD56 are NK-cell markers; the age-related NK change described is reduced perforin, granzymes, and activating receptors, not these T-cell molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD19 and CD21 are B-cell markers, not the T-cell signaling and co-stimulatory molecules that decline with age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD80 and CD86 are co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells; the age-related loss described is of CD28 on the T cell itself.
